sections.h2: What does the Seminole County tax roll look like?
sections.html:
The appraiser's 2026 statistics sketch the market that these records document. The county holds 181,187 real property parcels, of which 138,250 are residential, 6,923 commercial and 16,439 condominium. It also lists 13,489 tangible accounts and 45,960 apartment units. Taxable value totals about $60 billion against roughly $92 billion in market value.

The gap between those two totals is the effect of exemptions and assessment limits. Most of the paper moving through the records office in Sanford concerns those 138,000 residential parcels.

sections.h2: Which Seminole County office holds which record?
sections.html:
Three elected offices divide the records, and any given paper lives in just one.

  • Clerk and Comptroller: keeps the Official Records of recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, plats and maps, and also runs tax deed auctions.
  • Property Appraiser: ownership on the tax roll, value, exemptions and parcel data. The office is at 1101 E. 1st Street in downtown Sanford, open weekdays 8 to 5, with customer service at 407-665-7506 and exemption or fraud questions at 407-665-7512.
  • Tax Collector: bills, payments, installment plans and delinquent accounts.

A request to the wrong desk is simply redirected, but that costs days. The clerk's Official Records page lists what it holds: deeds, mortgages, notices of commencement, liens, condominium declarations, judgments, military discharges, probate papers, satisfactions and plats.

sections.h2: What are the ways to file a deed in Seminole County?
sections.html:
You can deliver it, mail it with fees and a self-addressed prepaid envelope, or send it electronically. The Official Records department is at 1750 E. Lake Mary Blvd., Sanford, FL 32773 (407-665-4405). Fees and stamp tax are paid when the document is filed.

The clerk says electronic submissions are typically recorded in 24 to 72 hours and that the image appears online afterward. Four approved vendors handle eRecording: CSC eRecording, eRecording Partners Network, Hopdox and Simplifile. The clerk suggests 300 DPI scans in TIFF or PDF, 8 by 11 pages, names indexed last name first, and no more than 15 documents per receipt.

Some items must be mailed or hand delivered instead: a notice of contest of lien or of bond, a notice of homestead, a transfer of liens to security by bond or cash, a transfer of judgment, and a notice of marketable title requiring a certificate of service.

sections.h2: What fees does the Seminole clerk post?
sections.html:
The posted sheet includes the stamp and tax lines that accompany a deed or mortgage, plus charges for copies and searches. The sheet repeats the state stamp rates, seventy cents per hundred dollars on a deed and thirty-five cents on a mortgage's secured amount, and adds a twenty cent intangible tax on mortgages. Per-page base charges come from section 28.24(13), plus trust fund and technology amounts the statute permits.

sections.h2: Can a flawed deed hold up a Seminole County sale?
sections.html:
Yes. Section 689.01 requires a signed writing with two witnesses, who may appear by audio-video link. A title company catches a missing witness, but curing it eats days.

State revenue guidance counts quitclaims, foreclosure-avoiding deeds and contracts for deed as taxable. Spousal homestead deeds backed only by a mortgage escape the tax, as do divorce transfers of the marital home and an estate representative's deed carrying out a probated will. Estate planning transfers get no blanket exemption.

sections.h2: How does the Seminole County Tax Collector bill and collect?
sections.html:
Once the appraiser certifies the roll, the collector prints and mails bills in November. The reward for paying promptly runs from 4 percent that month down to 1 percent in February, then nothing. The deadline is March 31; from April 1 the account is delinquent, payable only in certified funds, and picks up advertising and collection fees. Installment plans are offered, and a missed installment counts as delinquent on April 1.

Pay online, in person, by check to P.O. Box 630 in Sanford, or by courier at 1101 East First St, Room 1200. When a discount month ends on a weekend or legal holiday, the collector extends it to the next working day for payments delivered to a qualifying location.

The bill combines ad valorem millage set by taxing authorities with non-ad valorem assessments. The collector also explains that tangible taxes on business furniture, fixtures and equipment, and on rental property, arrive alongside the real estate bill and earn the same discounts.

sections.h2: What does Amendment 3 change for Seminole County owners?
sections.html:
The appraiser's homepage and the collector's tax page both report that voters approved the property tax amendment on November 3, 2026. The collector stresses that the 2026 bill stays as issued, nobody will receive a revised one, and the effects start with tax year 2027, billed in November 2027.

Valuation date stays January 1. The appraiser separates filing into a regular window, January 1 to March 1, and a pre-file window that runs March 2 through December 31 for the next year, and suggests pre-filing to dodge the lines. The standard homestead exemption reaches $50,000, the first $25,000 applying to every levy. A buyer is reassessed at just value on the January 1 after purchase.

sections.h2: How does a Seminole County tax deed sale work?
sections.html:
The clerk holds the auction and issues the deed to the top bidder. The holder of a tax certificate applies through the tax collector, and the process involves no lawsuit and no court order. The clerk cautions that such property sells buyer-beware and that the resulting deed carries no promise of clear, marketable title. Questions go to taxdeeds@seminoleclerk.org, and the auction calendar and files are online.

The statute makes a holder wait two years past the issue year's April 1 to apply. At the sale, the winner leaves a deposit that is not refundable, the greater of 5 percent and $200, and settles the balance within one business day. An owner behind on taxes should clear the account with the collector first.

sections.h2: What should a Seminole County owner check before selling?
sections.html:
• Search the Official Records for your deed and any mortgage, lien or judgment, trying every spelling of your name, since the index is only as accurate as the filings.
  • Make sure every paid-off mortgage has a recorded satisfaction.
  • Ask the appraiser to verify exemptions and parcel data. A parcel split or combination request waits until the current year's taxes are paid.
  • Ask the collector whether this year is paid.
  • List owner names exactly as on the deed for the new instrument.

If an old deed misspells a name, ask the clerk how a corrective instrument is recorded and what it costs. Cities such as Winter Springs, Oviedo and Lake Mary use the same county recording process. The clerk also offers free property fraud alerts, which the appraiser recommends.

faqs.q: Which office takes a Seminole County deed?
faqs.a: The clerk's Official Records department, 1750 E. Lake Mary Blvd. in Sanford. One office serves every city in the county.

faqs.q: What does the Seminole clerk charge to record?
faqs.a: Ten dollars for page one and $8.50 for each page after, with stamp taxes added where the document calls for them.

faqs.q: Does eRecording work for every document type?
faqs.a: No. A handful, including a notice of homestead and a transfer of judgment, have to be mailed or hand delivered.

faqs.q: Who holds Seminole County tax deed auctions?
faqs.a: The clerk. The certificate holder applies through the tax collector first.

faqs.q: On which day are Seminole bills late?
faqs.a: April 1, the day after the March 31 deadline. Late balances take certified funds and carry extra fees.
